newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street sentiment mixed over Clinton's address.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street sentiment mixed over Clinton's address.

text.p: Wall Street economists expressed mixed reactions to President Bill Clinton's State of the Union address on Tuesday, as his supportive call for a balanced budget by 2002 was tempered by blatant opposition to a constitutional amendment requiring the books to balance.

Financiers hoping to catch a glimpse of the Clinton administration's budget blueprint for fiscal 1998 were disappointed as the specifics were kept under wraps, awaiting Thursday's scheduled unveiling.

"It's a little bit tough to judge how the market is going to react to this speech, but lets put it this way -- the president is taking a centrist posture ... and his call for a balanced budget is likely to be met with some satisfaction by the bond market," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock and Co.
Clinton dashed some bond traders' wish for a more conciliatory stance over passage of a constitutional amendment, saying it could "cripple our country in time of crisis".

Republican congressional leaders, who fell just one vote short of passing a balanced budget amendment last year, have vowed to make it the first order of legislative business in the new Congress. The Senate is expected to begin debate on the amendment on Wednesday.

"There would be a positive reaction in the bond market to a constitutional amendment, beyond what there would be if we just came into agreement to balance the budget," said Dana Johnson, head of research at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc.
He added an amendment would reassure those market players wary of a resurgence of deficit financing even if the administration does manage to balance the books by 2002.
However, some economists applauded Clinton's opposition to the amendment and his effort to maintain fiscal policy flexiblity.
"Many economists are now against it," said Peter Kretzmer, an economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.
"The inflexiblility of the amendment could be a problem. I think now the momentum is against it and it won't pass both houses," he added.
Johnson said many economists question the wisdom of creating such "permanent restraints".
U.S. bond and stock market reaction on Wednesday to Clinton's address was expected to be limited.

U.S. debt and equity traders said they were reluctant to put large amounts at stake ahead of Wednesday's conclusion of a two-day Federal Reserve interest rate policy meeting. Also, the release of January U.S. payrolls data, scheduled for Friday, kept investors at bay, traders said.
Competing for the financial market's attention early on Wednesday will be the long-awaited verdict in the O.J. Simpson civil trial, which was announced near the end of Clinton's speech.
A civil jury blamed Simpson for the killings of his ex-wife and her friend and ordered him to pay $8.5 million in damages.

"I was in the car coming home, stuck in traffic, and all I heard on the radio was O.J., O.J., O.J. I thought perhaps the president had got the boot until after the verdict," said a San Francisco-based portfolio manager. "This will be the market talk tomorrow, not Clinton," the money manager added.
